Executive Summary 
Uncertainty the only certainty 
• Our view of the fundamentals has shifted slightly since the last quarterly.  We are now 
expecting that refined consumption will be higher in 2012 but lower in 2013 than we did in 
April, mainly in China due to scrap market effects.  This is on top of our continued 
assumption of an acceleration in consumption growth in H2 in China, as economic policy is 
loosened and infrastructure focused stimulus measures boost copper end-use demand. 
• With refined production forecast to be higher than three months ago in both 2012 and 2013, 
our deficit forecast for this year has been trimmed to below 500,000t and the April forecast 
of a 150,000t deficit next year has been converted into a balanced market. 
• When looked at on a China/World ex-China basis in 2012 the picture is one of a surplus in 
the former and a deficit in the latter.  The small Chinese surplus comes from lower imports 
in H2 creating a deficit in the period to reduce the excess stocks built up in Q1.  An annual 
deficit of over 600,000t in the World ex-China was assured when Q1 alone saw a deficit of 
almost 570,000t.  Record Chinese cathode imports in Q1 this year were supplied by imports 
from all major producing countries, suggesting that producers drew down stocks. 
• For their part, investors have turned bearish due to on-going concerns over the Eurozone 
crisis and the economic outlook in general.  As a result, they sold copper and other 
commodities over the past three months.  Both fundamental and financial factors have come 
together to reduce the 2012 price forecast to just under $8,000/t ($3.60/lb). 
• In 2013, as the Chinese economy accelerates and the macroeconomic picture is expected to 
improve in the rest of the world, we forecast that the price will rise to an average of $8,500/t 
($3.85/lb), peaking in Q2 before drifting lower through H2. 
• World consumption growth is forecast to peak in 2014.  With some mine projects shifted 
into later years, refined production will grow by less than consumption, tipping the market 
back into a small deficit.  In 2015 and 2016, rapidly rising output from mine projects will 
boost refined supply and the market will move into a period of sustained surplus.  As stocks 
increase the price will come down to an annual average below $7,350/t ($3.33/lb) by 2016.

Copper Quarterly July 2012   Executive Summary 
CRU International Limited confidential 
Macroeconomic outlook remains in the driving seat 
We forecast that the copper market will be in a deficit of almost 500,000t in 2012, as mine and 
refined production growth will be minimal compared to a more than 3% increase in consumption.  
The macroeconomic picture, and therefore copper consumption prospects, is at a critical juncture 
in the economic cycle, due to the Eurozone crisis and questions about Chinese and US growth 
prospects.  As a result, uncertainty over the direction of the economy is overshadowing copper 
fundamentals, as well as dictating the ebb and flow of sentiment among financial players.  The 
only fundamentals that have affected prices recently, and which we expect to continue to do so in 
the near term, are the relatively low levels of exchange stocks. 
The twists and turns of the copper price in May and June exemplify the impact of these factors 
on the market.  The 3-month price on the LME fell to a low for the year of $7,270/t on 8th June 
from a recent high of $8,440/t on 1st May.  The May high and subsequent decline was due in part 
to the backwardation that followed the largest ever one day cancellation of warrants on the LME 
on 20th April.  The cancellation was rumoured to be the work of a large trader and is reported to 
have caught Chinese smelters short.  They responded by exporting cathode to LME warehouses in 
Asia in May and early June, helping to achieve record monthly exports in May of 102,375t. 
Another apparent anomaly in the trade data was the fact that US imports into China reached a 
new record amount of over 30,000t of cathode in May.  This followed a then record US monthly 
import of almost 16,000t in April and in turn was followed by over 18,000t arriving from the US 
in June.  These shipments help explain the drawdown in exchange stocks in the US in Q1.  
However, the large negative arbitrage meant that someone suffered a high opportunity cost. 
The price also fell by the beginning of June as investors took a cautious approach and moved 
money into “safer” assets than copper as they awaited the outcome of the latest Greek election.  In 
the end the results of the Greek election were as positive as could be expected and the copper price 
Major changes since the April 2012 Quarterly report 
Demand: Upward revisions to North American and European 2011 consumption have 
been offset by downward shifts to South & Central America (C&SA) and Other Asia.  In 
2012 the forecast has been raised by 150,000t due to the base effect of a higher 2011 in 
North America and Europe, as well as more consumption in China, which are offset only 
marginally by lower base effects in C&SA and Other Asia.  For 2013, Chinese and North 
American consumption have been revised down due to scrap effects, leaving a 115,000t 
lower total figure.  We have a cumulative 275,000t higher consumption forecast for 2014-
2016, almost wholly due to higher Chinese consumption growth. 
Supply: Further upward revisions to 2011 mine output mean that refined production is 
220,000t higher than previously estimated.  Potential refined production has been lowered in 
2012 but higher mine production means that the actual forecast output is 220,000t above the 
April level.  More mine production in 2013 and 2015-16 is only minimally offset by a 
150,000t reduction in 2014 output due to shifting forward of some probable and possible 
projects, leaving a cumulative 265,000t increase in refined output between 2013 and 2016. 
Prices: Prices for 2012 have been lowered by another $550/t and by $690/t in 2013 as a 
result of a slower decline in stocks to critically low levels and lower investor buying.  The 
reduction in price is not as great in 2014-16, ranging from $370/t lower in 2015 and only 
$150/t in 2016, as stocks rise to similar levels forecast in the April report.

the end of the month, the results of the Eurozone summit on 28th June boosted sentiment among 
financial investors following the softening of German Chancellor Angela Merkel’s stance against

China semis growth drives stronger copper consumption 
With stocks relatively low and refined supply growth constrained until projects begin to 
significantly raise mine output next year, the focus of attention in analysing the near term 
fundamentals is on the demand side.  In this context, China’s potential economic growth is the key 
driver.  Semis production growth was up by an estimated 16.2% y-o-y in H1 2012, but was down 
0.5% on H2 2011.  The decline in prices in Q2 and the negative SHFE-LME arbitrage discouraged 
scrap imports, which decreased by 3.0% y-o-y based on our contained copper estimate.  However, 
scrap held back by traders in Q4 as a result of the decline in the copper price in October seems to 
have been released in H1 2012.  This led to real consumption of refined metal growing by “only” 
11% y-o-y but falling by 3.8% on H2 2011, while scrap grew by an estimated 8.6% on H2 2011. 
On the economy front, the slowdown engineered in economic growth over the past year in 
China has contained the property bubble that had developed as a result of stimulus spending in 
2008-2009.  However, the property market remains a cause for concern for the authorities, as 
property prices in the large cities have not fallen as much as in rural areas.  Therefore, the central 
government, as it continues to loosen monetary policy following the successful reining in of 
inflationary pressure, will seek to control lending by limiting credit to property but relaxing it for 
other sectors.  Interest rates for benchmark deposit rates and lending rates have already been 
reduced and the June data on bank lending show that it has increased relative to May.  These 
looser monetary conditions mean that the collateral stock trade, in which investors use copper as a 
financing tool to circumvent limits on credit, has been reduced.  Nevertheless, stocks in bonded 
warehouses remain elevated as imports fell in June, but imports are still above the monthly 
average level required to meet the shortfall in supply from domestic refineries.

copper demand from the construction sector.  In addition, the government is targeting 
infrastructure development for a round of stimulus spending that will be supportive.  The 
announcement of subsidies for energy efficient home appliances and fuel efficient cars will only 
have a marginal impact on copper demand.  The subsidies introduced in 2009 and sustained 
through last year brought forward too much demand for appliances for the latest subsidies to 
promote large scale additional buying by consumers. 
As industrial production growth accelerates from 9.7% y-o-y in Q2 to 12.6% by Q4 and the 
above policy measures feed through, we expect copper consumption in China to pick up 
sequentially in H2 2012.  We forecast that refined consumption will rise from 1.9Mt in Q1 to 
2.1Mt by the final quarter of the year and register a 7.2% increase for the full year, versus the 
6.3% that we forecast in the April Quarterly.  In 2013, we expect that as the economic activity 
picks up, scrap availability will rise in countries that export to China.  Higher use of scrap will 
lead to slightly slower growth in refined consumption in China of 6.0%, despite industrial 
production ticking up from 11.4% this year to 12.5% in 2013. 
European consumption growth down… 
We forecast that refined copper consumption in the World ex-China will rise by 1.0% in 2012, 
before rising to only 2.1% in 2013.  However, behind the headline figures, European growth is 
expected to be a drag on growth this year, after supporting consumption in 2011, with the rest of 
the world doing the opposite – supporting growth this year after limiting it in 2011. 
Europe and how it manages its twin banking and sovereign debt crises remains the largest 
single source of uncertainty about the demand outlook.  As we expected three months ago, 
conditions have deteriorated.  Northern countries are still doing much better than those in the 
south.  However, the momentum in the north has slowed as the seemingly interminable wrangling 
over debt reduction and austerity measures saps consumer and business confidence.  European

…but rest of World bounces back from 2011 decline 
As noted above, the rest of the world hindered growth in 2011 but is now bouncing back to 
support consumption this year.  Within this overall picture, the US has seen mixed developments 
over the past few months.  The new SDI-La Farga wirerod plant that began operation in June will 
be a drag on refined consumption in North America, as its production displaces that of other 
regional wirerod producers.  On the positive side, the auto sector continues to perform well, with 
Ford and Chrysler reporting that they will limit summer shutdowns at their plants to meet the 
sustained demand for new vehicles in the country.  However, the position of the all-important 
construction sector remains gloomy.  There have been some flickers of an upturn for several 
months, but the overhang of homeowners with negative equity is huge, as is the number of empty 
homes.  Until these are cleared rates of growth in residential construction activity will remain 
subdued.  Overall, we expect that refined consumption will rise by 3.3% in the US, following last 
year’s 0.4% decline.  Next year, decelerating North American industrial production plus the full 
impact of the SDI-La Farga mill will lead to regional consumption declining by 1.6%. 
Central & South American refined consumption growth is on course to grow by 4.8% this year, 
as Brazil recovers from its downturn in 2011.  In 2013, Brazilian preparations for the World Cup 
in 2014 and Olympics in 2016 are expected to gather pace.  Therefore, copper consumption in the 
region will accelerate to 6.0%.

semis imports, refined copper consumption in the rest of Asia is suffering, particularly in the 
major exporters Taiwan and South Korea.  The Thai floods dragged down copper consumption in

whole we forecast a modest rise of just 1.5%.  In Japan, subsidies for fuel efficient cars are 
boosting auto demand, including for copper.  The Japanese Electric Wire & Cable Makers’ 
Association reported that shipments to the auto sector rose by 36.3% y-o-y in June.  However, this

Investors will continue to react very quickly to developments in the Eurozone crisis.  As a 
result, we have seen and will continue to see high levels of price volatility, which is not the ideal 
environment to encourage a longer-term commitment from commodity investors.  Instead, they 
will look for a clear sign of stability in the euro before having the confidence to commit their

Key risks to the price outlook 
In 2012, risks to the price around the base case are fairly balanced, as the range forecast in the 
chart above demonstrates.  The range is wider than in previous quarterlies, as we have widened the 
bands to better reflect historical copper price ranges.  Downside macroeconomic and financial 
risks and their consequent negative impact on consumption are offsetting the upside risks of lower 
copper production and higher investor inflows into copper.  One point to note is that Chinese 
buying as the price falls below $7,000/t provides a floor for the price.  In 2013, as the forecast is 
lower than in April, the risks remain symmetrical.  From 2014 to 2016, the risks become biased to 
the high side, as production risks come to the fore, driven principally by production possibly 
underperforming compared to the base case.  The downside risks come from demand significantly 
underperforming the base through some form of intensified economic disruptions, most likely 
driven by another financial sector shock. 
Production risks 
Production risks to the price are mostly to the upside.  The first is that tight availability of 
equipment, qualified personnel, water, power, etc. mean that sequencing of projects (at both the 
company and industry levels) will be a serious challenge.  We believe that there is a greater 
downside than upside risk to our production forecast and therefore an upward bias to the price 
forecast, especially in the 2014-16 period, when there is significant risk that mine projects will not 
come on as expected in the base case. 
There is some downside risk from production.  We have a mine disruption allowance in the 
2014-2016 period of 12-13% and have made allowances for project risks of a 10% 
underperformance for firm projects, 30% for probable and 60% for possible ones.  If our 
macroeconomic forecast turns out to be too optimistic, then demand could be less and the wave of 
mine projects could come on just in time to swamp the market and drive down prices sooner than 
in our base case. 
Macroeconomic and financial risks 
The key risk to the copper price is the uncertainty of how the global economy will perform.  
The apparent improvement in the US could prove short-lived and China could possibly not see a 
return to growth in H2 2012.  The Eurozone crisis could also still prompt more financial market

Downside 
Aluminium producers are currently facing challenging conditions, with the industry in a 
situation of chronic oversupply.  Smelter closures began in the beginning of 2012, with many of 
the closures directly impacting captive hot metal wirerod plants at aluminium smelters.  So, 
despite a Cu:Al price ratio of almost 4:1, supply constraints are likely to prevent aluminium from 
increasing its market share in the rod sector in the short term.  Longer term though, the 
substitution threat remains significant for copper demand growth in wirerod.  We expect 
aluminium will make more inroads into the insulated power cable market as a result of an increase 
in aluminium wirerod capacity available to target this segment by 2015. 
CRU forecasts that the ratio of the copper price to that of aluminium will average close to 4:1, 
which will weigh on all consumers’ strategic decision-making regarding substituting away from 
copper. 
Upside 
The potential shortage of scrap for direct use (due to weaker generation) could lead to 
additional cathode requirements, especially in China. 
A double-dip recession would only accelerate the emerging markets decoupling their economic 
growth further from the industrialised countries by favouring copper-intensive domestic demand. 
Some Chinese consumers or the SRB could see copper as a bargain for speculative purposes at 
prices much lower than our base case, thus leading to higher cathode imports.  As a result of RMB 
appreciation, further support for copper could also emerge from a diversion of surplus cash away

2.1   Refined consumption overview 
Since the April issue of the Copper Quarterly, we have revised up world refined copper 
consumption in 2012 by 153,000t.  Global growth this year in copper cathode demand is set to

Direct revisions were made to some annual volumes.  In order of greatest to least change in 
volume, these were: Russia, up 69kt in 2011 and similar positive corrections in subsequent

2014-16 on scrap and the percentage-growth from a higher base; South Korea, down 45kt in

were more minor annual adjustments made to changes to Greece, Italy, Spain, Sweden, 
Canada, Chile, Egypt, South Africa, India, Japan, Thailand and Vietnam. 
The continuing debt-crisis in Europe and slower economic growth in China has led to some very 
negative sentiment on the prospects for refined copper demand this year.  Our base case 
assumes that the European economy will not collapse nor worsen significantly and that China 
will meet its GDP growth target of 7.5% y-o-y in 2012.  In 2012, growth in copper cathode 
consumption will be driven by China, which is expected to rise by 7.2% y-o-y, supported by a 
relaxation in monetary policies, together with infrastructural and housing investment, targeted 
subsidies and a tightened scrap market at least until the end of Q3.   
North American copper demand has also been strong and we expect full year refined demand 
growth of 2.1% y-o-y, supported by growth in the US automotive industry, electrical 
infrastructure and industrial sectors.  However, this growth may have been greater without the 
rise in scrap usage in North America with the introduction of SDI-La Farga‟s new wirerod mill.

Distortions imposed by the scrap market 
Changes in copper semis demand can on the most part be reduced to the impact of changes in 
end use demand, as reflected by the close growth relationship it has with global industrial 
production growth.  However, copper cathode demand is more volatile and has a different 
growth pattern to end use demand.  The principal factor that distorts this relationship is the use 
of copper scrap in semis production.  We estimate that direct scrap usage in the copper semis 
fabrication industry accounted for 21% of total semis production in 2011.  Material availability 
differences in the cathode and copper scrap market means that relative usage varies from year-
to-year, which often lead to much lower or higher refined copper consumption compared to 
changes in end-use demand. 
An important difference between the cathode and scrap supply is its price elasticity.  Copper 
cathode supply is relatively price inelastic compared to copper scrap supply.  A change in the 
relevant metal exchange‟s copper spot delivery price therefore has different effects upon copper 
cathode and copper scrap availability.  Copper cathode availability does not respond to changes 
in the price level very much as most consumers are hedged and pass the costs downstream.  
However, copper scrap availability responds very rapidly to changes in the price level because 
there is a larger proportion of scrap merchants who are exposed to changes in the price.  When 
the copper price falls, they are left with „expensive‟ material which is stocked until the price 
rises once again.  When the price rises they release those expensive stocks until the price falls or 
the stocks are depleted.  The effect of this is that changes in copper scrap prices tend to be less 
than changes in copper cathode prices.  This means that in a rising copper price scenario, scrap 
supply is good, and the widening price difference from cathode means that it is favourable for

International trade in copper scrap tends to exaggerate the change in scrap availability due to 
price changes.  There is trade data to suggest that China, as a major importer of scrap, has 
encountered this phenomenon a number of times.  The copper price had been on an upward 
trend from 2009 to early-2011 but then collapsed in October 2011.  Whilst prices rose in 2010, 
merchants imported growing amounts of scrap resulting in the level of scrap availability rising 
and resulting in a 61% stimulated rise in scrap and alloy metal consumption in H2 2010 
compared to H1.  However, the copper price peaked in February and continued a downward 
(albeit volatile) trend through to Q4 2011 when it collapsed to below US$7,000/t.  This 
squeezed the scrap market, as merchants withdrew any imports purchased at a higher price and 
scrap consumption decreased by an estimated 24% and 19% period-on-period in H1 and H2 
2011.  Imports of copper scrap over this period still remained at similar levels to the previous 
year.  Since the level of consumption of high grade scrap and alloy material was falling, but 
copper scrap import volumes remained at a high level and at an equivalent grade, scrap 
merchants stockpiles must have grown considerably. 
As prices rose in Q1 scrap merchant stocks were made available once again, loosening the scrap 
market but seeing to a large rise in scrap and alloy metal consumption of an estimated 68% q-o-
q, despite the weaker semis demand associated with the Spring Festival early in Q1.  As copper 
prices recovered slightly in Q2, the scrap market again tightened and scrap consumption 
responded accordingly, dropping 17% in Apr-May on the previous two-month period. 
These swings in scrap consumption cause changes in the use of copper cathode and through 
most of 2011, the tight scrap market resulted in elevated levels of cathode consumption in China 
despite slower Chinese semis growth.

3.3.1 North East Asia 
Activity of the copper consuming industries in South Korea and Taiwan was lower than 
expected in 2011.  Apparent consumption figures for copper cathode revealed that South Korean 
demand contracted by 15.4% y-o-y, to reach 775,000t and similarly, in Taiwan, demand fell by 
14% y-o-y to reach 459,000t in 2011.  Due to this data and the impact of some Korean 
consumer destocking activity, CRU has revised the South Korean and Taiwanese consumption 
to 816,000t and 459,000t in 2011, representing annual declines of -10.0% and -14.0%, 
respectively. 
We principally attribute the fast reduction in copper demand to a number of structural factors, 
including the historically close copper semis trade relationship that these nations had with 
China, the migration of Taiwanese downstream copper consuming companies towards China for 
competitive purposes and the growth of local Chinese semi-fabrication capacity.  In addition to 
these structural factors, domestic demand for copper products has also been particularly weak in 
South Korea. 
Looking at these factors in more detail yields insight into how these related industries are 
developing.  Semis production in Taiwan remains highly geared toward China, however the 
ratio of semi-finished copper products destined for China from Taiwan has been shrinking.  In 
2008, 39% of Taiwanese shipments were exported to its neighbour.  However, this figure had 
contracted to 32% in 2011.  We attribute this change to the Chinese industry‟s wirerod capacity 
expansion.  Exports of wirerod to China now only account for 13% of Taiwanese overseas 
shipments.  This contrasts with brass mill semi-finished products, where 56% of Taiwan‟s 
shipments travel to China and 80% of the total to export destinations in general.  This means

3.3.2 China 
Demand for copper in China remained subdued throughout H1 2012.  As reported in the 
previous issue, the usual sustained growth in copper demand following the Chinese Lunar New 
Year did not occur.  This was partially as a consequence of the less pronounced seasonal dip in 
refined consumption during the holiday month but was also related to weaker y-o-y growth in 
underlying economic activity.  Industrial production expanded by 11.6% y-o-y in Q1, slowing 
from the rate of growth seen in the same period of the previous year of 14.8% y-o-y.  
Furthermore, IP growth slowed again in Q2, registering 9.7% y-o-y, the weakest growth 
performance in China since Q2 2009.  Fixed asset investment statistics from the National 
Bureau of Statistics of China indicate strong overall growth of 20.1% year-to-date for Jan-May 
2012, supporting copper demand.  Interest rate cuts in June and July, as well as a reduction in 
banks reserve ratio and the introduction of new stimulus policies, promise faster growth for 
period-on-period copper consumption in H2 2012.  This has already impacted the 
manufacturing sector, July PMI‟s for which showed renewed activity after 5 months of 
contraction.

The Chinese copper fabrication industry has also been contending with increasing competition 
and the associated rise in industry production capacity.  As total copper consumption has been 
weaker than expected, there has been divergence between the rate of industry expansion and the 
rate of orders, impacting on operating rates.  Statistics on utilisation rates tend to differ 
substantially depending on the type of semis products it considers and also the diversity of the 
survey group.  For example, in April, we heard that large fabricators had not experienced as 
severe a drop in operating rates as their smaller capacity rivals.  Larger fabricators tend to be 
State-owned enterprises and have the capability to handle big public sector contracts.  This 
position has allowed them to take advantage of new investment in the power and social housing 
sectors, which continued to be major sources of support for the copper products manufacturers

approximately matched capacity to demand as it has consolidated into a number of large 
companies.  In contrast to this, the copper PSS industry is relatively young, with domestic 
production beginning in earnest around 2006.  As such, the industry remains fragmented and 
capacity is being installed at a furious pace, leaving participants vulnerable to any weakness in

A positive factor for copper demand both in H2 2012 and in the medium term comes from the 
railway sector.  The Ministry of Railways is trying to restart plans to build-out 85 urban railway 
lines across more than 30 cities with a total length of 2,700km by 2015.  The ministry had 
shelved the plans following the withdrawal of central government‟s funding for the projects 
following the high-speed train crash tragedy that took place on 23rd July 2011.  However, the 
ministry has since introduced measures to raise funds by itself: RMB20B through issuance of a 
bond and also a RMB2.0 trillion credit line, which was granted by banks last year.  It is 
therefore likely that the rail sector will become the largest driver of growth in the coming years.  
In addition to this, reports from early July indicated that the ministry had only spent RMB148B 
of an annual railway budget worth RMB448B, leaving room for a significant boost in copper 
consumption for H2 2012.  As of early May, the ministry reported that it had 96 urban rail lines 
under construction in 16 cities with a total operating length of 2,200km.  In recent years, railway 
transport construction has averaged 270km per annum.
